passage: Two hours before the last bus, and Aditi's exam on cell biology was at nine tomorrow. The hostel corridor was loud with a birthday party. She had the chat open on the phone, a video playing on the laptop with the sound low, headphones on with a playlist, and the textbook under her elbow. Every few minutes she answered a message, glanced at a scene, changed the song. She felt busy, very busy. Tushar leaned in and asked, “Quick: what does the mitochondrion do?” Aditi opened her mouth and found nothing. Two hours of “studying”, and she had absorbed one page. She shut the laptop lid, slowly.

qa.q: When was Aditi's exam on cell biology?
qa.a: Aditi's exam on cell biology was at nine tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Aditi feel when she opened her mouth and found nothing?
qa.a: Aditi felt shocked and a little dismayed: she had felt busy for two hours but could not answer one simple question.

qa.q: What could Aditi try in the next hour to make the study count?
qa.a: Close the chat and video, keep one song or none, and study the one topic in short blocks before checking any messages.

qa.q: How might Tushar see Aditi's blank pause?
qa.a: Tushar might feel surprised and sympathetic, since Aditi looked so busy, and may realise the quiet question showed how little had stayed.

grounding: A student studies with chat, music and videos running and feels busy while retaining little.

passage: At the corner table of the café, Mehak had her laptop with two chats open, a lecture video paused and restarted, and a lo-fi playlist. She typed notes, read a message, typed another line, glanced at the video. The tea had gone cold. After two hours, Abhinav, who had been reading quietly across the table, looked up. “Give me the summary of that chapter?” he asked. Mehak began, stopped, and looked at her notes. They were full of half-sentences. “I was doing so much,” she said, mostly to herself. Abhinav shrugged kindly. “Try one thing at a time, then tell me.” She closed everything but the notes.

qa.q: How long had Mehak been working when Abhinav looked up?
qa.a: Mehak had been working for two hours when Abhinav looked up.

qa.q: What did Mehak feel when she looked at her half-sentence notes?
qa.a: Mehak felt surprised and a little disappointed, since the effort of switching had felt like real work but had left little behind.

qa.q: What could Mehak try next to make the notes useful?
qa.a: Close the chats and the video, read one section, and write it in her own words before moving on.

qa.q: How might Abhinav be feeling when he asks for the summary?
qa.a: Abhinav is probably curious and friendly, and his kind shrug suggests he means to help, not embarrass Mehak.

grounding: A student studies with chat, music and videos and mistakes switching effort for progress.

passage: Ganga, nineteen, studied for her BCom exams in her family's small house in Mandya. She liked to think she was efficient. Her phone played songs, a video lecture ran on the laptop, and her class group chat pinged every minute. She answered Sabina about the bus timings, typed notes, sang along, replied again. At ten she closed the laptop, satisfied: four hours of work. The next morning, Sabina quizzed her on the accounting chapter over tea. Ganga couldn't explain depreciation, which she had "studied" last night. Her face fell. That evening she tried one hour with only the book. She remembered more from that hour than from the four before.

qa.q: Which chapter did Sabina quiz Ganga on?
qa.a: Sabina quizzed her on the accounting chapter.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when she couldn't explain depreciation?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and a little shocked, since she had felt so busy and efficient the night before.

qa.q: What would you advise Ganga for her next study session?
qa.a: Study with only the book for a set time, and answer chats and play music afterwards, since switching every minute left little behind.

qa.q: How is Sabina affected by Ganga's study style?
qa.a: Sabina gets quick replies about bus timings, but also sees, through the quiz, that Ganga didn't really learn the chapter.

grounding: Shows a student studying with chat, music and video at once, feeling busy while retaining little.

passage: Yuki, twenty, had a history test at her university in Osaka. On Sunday afternoon she spread out her notes, opened a music playlist, kept a drama episode running in a small window "for background" and replied to Aiko's messages about a festival. She felt productive, like she was doing four things well. By evening she had highlighted thirty pages. On Monday, halfway through the test, she stared at a question about the treaty she had highlighted in bright yellow. Nothing came. Walking out, she told Aiko, "I was so busy. How did I learn nothing?" Aiko said, "You were busy switching." Yuki thought about that all the way home.

qa.q: How many pages had Yuki highlighted by evening?
qa.a: She had highlighted thirty pages.

qa.q: What was Yuki feeling when she walked out of the test?
qa.a: She felt confused and frustrated, having felt busy all Sunday yet unable to recall the treaty.

qa.q: What went wrong in Yuki's study session, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Constant switching between notes, music, drama and chat made her feel busy but left little in memory; studying one thing at a time could fix it.

qa.q: How does Aiko see Yuki's Sunday?
qa.a: Aiko sees it plainly as switching, not studying, and says so directly.

grounding: Shows a student running music, video and chat while studying and mistaking busy switching for progress.

passage: In the university library's group room, Urmila had three windows open: her economics notes, a chat with her project group and a comedy clip. Earphones played music. Madhav, across the table, watched her flick between them every few seconds. After two hours, he asked, "What's elasticity?" She laughed. "I just read that." She tried to explain and stopped. "Wait." He slid his phone into his bag. "Try forty minutes, notes only. Then we'll check messages together." She groaned, but closed the chat. At the end, she explained elasticity in two sentences and felt a small, surprised pride. "Okay. That's annoying," she said, smiling.

qa.q: How many windows did Urmila have open?
qa.a: She had three windows open.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling when she explained elasticity at the end?
qa.a: She felt a small, surprised pride, and a little amused annoyance that the single-task approach had worked.

qa.q: Which change helped Urmila, and why?
qa.a: Forty minutes with notes only removed the constant switching, so she actually retained what she read.

qa.q: How might Madhav have felt watching Urmila flick between windows?
qa.a: Madhav may have felt concerned and a bit amused, seeing that all the activity wasn't turning into learning.

grounding: Shows a student in a library feeling busy with many windows open but retaining little until she single-tasks.

passage:
Dear Minakshi,
You asked how I study so much and still have time to chat. Here's the embarrassing truth: I don't.
Until last week, my "study" looked like this: lecture video playing, two chats open, music in one ear, notes in a doc, and a shopping tab for new shoes. I'd switch every minute. I felt incredibly busy. At the end of three hours, I'd feel tired, like I'd worked hard.
Then we had the economics quiz. I'd "studied" that chapter for two evenings. I got four out of fifteen. I couldn't remember a single graph.
My professor said something about switching: each time you jump to a chat and back, you lose a little, and the losses add up. The tiredness is from switching, not learning.
So this week I tried one tab, no music, forty minutes. It felt slow and boring. But I remembered it the next day.
I'll reply to your messages at nine now, I promise.
Parul

qa.q: What did Parul score in the economics quiz?
qa.a: I got four out of fifteen.

qa.q: How did Parul feel after three hours of multitasking?
qa.a: Parul felt tired and busy, as if a lot of hard work had been done.

qa.q: What change did Parul try, and why does it help?
qa.a: One tab, no music, forty minutes, because it avoids the small losses from switching and lets the learning stick.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Minakshi might feel amused and a little surprised, and perhaps curious to try the same forty-minute focus.

grounding: Illustrates a student who studies with chats, music and videos running, feels busy and retains little, then tries single-task focus.
